offered_action_specs.name: rollback_deploy
offered_action_specs.description: Roll one service back to the settings it ran before its latest deploy, as the deploy log records them. Code plans it from that log, not from your tools' results, so you can name it even when they cannot see deploys: if the log holds no deploy of that service to undo, or the service changed since, code refuses it. Its container is recreated, so the service pauses while it restarts. Money already booked wrong stays wrong: a rollback stops new damage, and repairs nothing.

proposed.why: No tool calls are left; the results point to database pool exhaustion after the 19:38:23 payments-api deploy, with the leak's mechanism inferred, not shown.

findings.cause: payments-api ran out of PostgreSQL connections. The container was recreated at 19:38:23 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. About 35 s later the first 500s appear, and every sampled 500 is psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout: requests wait about 6 s for a connection, then fail. POST /payments goes from about 3.5 s⁻¹ of 201s to 0 and 7.7 s⁻¹ of 500s, which matches the alert's error rate and latency. Provider calls stay fast (p95 under 10 ms), so slow provider calls are not holding the connections. The most likely mechanism is that the refund path, under REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, keeps or leaks its pooled connection. Each refund then removes one connection until the pool is empty, and after that payments and refunds both time out. This mechanism is inferred from the setting's name and the timing; no tool showed the connections held.

evidence.shows: POST /payments: 500s start at 19:39:07 (0.125 s⁻¹) and reach 4.75 s⁻¹ at 19:39:37, while 201s fall from 3.5 to 0.5 s⁻¹. This confirms the alert.
payments-api was recreated at 19:38:23 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, PROVIDER_BREAKER=on and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents. Every other service was created at 19:36:56.
All sampled payments-api errors from 19:39:38 to 19:39:40 are PoolTimeout (psycopg pool) on POST /payments.
Many POST /payments traces and one refund trace from about 19:39:04 last about 6 to 6.8 s, which accounts for the p95 latency.
A refund trace lasts 6.8 s and ends in a 500 with psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout. It has no DB or provider spans, only Redis spans: it waited the whole time for a connection.
payments-api p95 to the provider is about 5 to 30 ms throughout, so provider slowness is ruled out.
Refunds ran at 0.2 to 0.4 s⁻¹ with 201s from 19:37:29. 500s on both routes start together at 19:38:59, about 35 s after the deploy, which fits a pool being slowly drained. All 201s then stop.

findings.left_open: No tool showed which code holds the connections, or that REFUND_CONNECTION=kept leaks one per refund; that link comes from the setting's name and the timing. Pool size and pool metrics were not queried. Other causes of exhaustion were not ruled out, such as idle-in-transaction sessions, Postgres-side limits or a load increase: payment traffic did ramp up from 19:37. Postgres health and service_health were not checked. Whether failed payments left partial state (Redis idempotency keys set before the 500s) was not checked, and money_check was not run.

proposed.why: The results support pool exhaustion in payments-api that starts right after its 19:38:23 recreation. The REFUND_CONNECTION=kept leak is the most likely mechanism, and a rollback both tests it and stops the damage.

diagnosis.hypothesis: payments-api's psycopg connection pool ran dry after the container was recreated at 19:38:23 with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept. The likely mechanism is that each refund keeps its pooled connection and never returns it. Refunds ran at about 0.3-0.4/s, so roughly 10-15 connections were gone within about 35 s. Then every request waited the pool timeout (about 6 s) and failed with PoolTimeout. That gives the 5xx share and the 7.4 s p95. Retries then roughly doubled the request rate. Unproven: no result shows the pool size, which code holds the connections, or the settings before the deploy. The provider is fast throughout. Payment load had levelled off before the failures began, so a load surge does not explain them.

evidence.shows: payments-api is the only service recreated recently, at 19:38:23, with REFUND_CONNECTION=kept, PROVIDER_BREAKER=on and CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents. Every other service dates from 19:36:56. The result does not show the previous settings, so it does not prove which setting changed.

Refund and payment 201s ran fine from 19:37:29, before the deploy. 500s on both routes first appear at 19:38:59, about 35 s after the deploy. Payment 201s had levelled off at about 3.5/s by 19:38:29, then fell to 0. 500s rose to 7.7/s, about twice the earlier success rate, which suggests retries. 409s rose too.
The 5-minute view of POST /payments matches: 500s start at 19:39:07 and reach 4.75/s while 201s collapse. This confirms the alert's error rate.
Every sampled ERROR log line between 19:39:38 and 19:39:40 is exception_type PoolTimeout on POST /payments, raised from a worker thread.
The slow traces from about 19:39:03 last 5.9-6.8 s, both POST /payments and a refund. This is consistent with a fixed pool wait timeout and explains the p95.
A refund trace ends in a 500 with psycopg_pool.PoolTimeout after 6.8 s. It has no DB or provider spans, only a Redis SET and a final EVAL, so it spent its whole life waiting for a connection.
A failed payment trace has only a Redis SET, the idempotency key, and never reaches the DB. Partial idempotency state is possible.
payments-api's outbound HTTP p95 to the provider stays at about 5-30 ms throughout, so slow provider calls are not holding connections.

proposed_fix.summary: Roll payments-api back to the settings it ran before the 19:38:23 deploy. The recreated container starts with a fresh pool, and the refund path stops holding connections, assuming REFUND_CONNECTION was the change. Afterwards, watch POST /payments and refund 5xx and p95 for several minutes while refunds flow. If PoolTimeouts return, the cause lies elsewhere: check Postgres sessions and limits and the pool size. Then run the money check and look for orphaned idempotency keys in Redis from the failed requests.

diagnosis.blast_radius: payments-api pauses while its container is recreated, and in-flight payments and refunds fail. Clients retry, and idempotency keys should cover the retries. The rollback restores all of the previous settings, not just REFUND_CONNECTION. If the earlier PROVIDER_BREAKER or CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT values differ, charge amounts or breaker behaviour could change too: check the deploy log diff before approving. The rollback repairs nothing already done wrong, such as requests that failed with keys still set in Redis.
diagnosis.rollback_plan: Redeploy payments-api with the current settings (PROVIDER_BREAKER=on, CHARGE_AMOUNT_UNIT=cents, REFUND_CONNECTION=kept) from the deploy log. This brings back the current failure mode, so do it only if the rolled-back settings turn out worse, for example wrong charge units.
